hints: Focus on the microscope itself: a simple light microscope at x400 with daylight has limited resolving power, so ask which of these four structures is large and dense enough to stand out.

Remember the light microscope resolution limit is about 200 nm (0.2 micrometres), so tiny ultrastructure like ribosomes and grana membranes will blur out, while a stained, large structure inside the nucleus will show clearly.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a light microscope can do**

Think of the light microscope as great for cells and large organelles, but not for fine ultrastructure. Its best resolution is about $0.2 \mu m$ and x400 is a standard high-power school magnification.

Key rule:
$$\text{light microscope limit} \approx 200 \, nm$$

**Sort the options by size**

Ribosomes are tiny at about $20 \, nm$, grana thylakoids are also nanometre-scale membranes, and lysosomes are very small vesicles around $0.1$ to $0.5 \, \mu m$. Nucleoli are much larger, dense bodies $1$ to $2 \, \mu m$ across inside the nucleus, and they stain strongly.

**Pick what is clearly visible**

At x400 with stain, you will see the cell wall, nucleus, vacuole and chloroplasts as whole organelles, plus the dark nucleolus inside the nucleus. You will not resolve internal chloroplast membranes or tiny ribosomes and lysosomes clearly, so C is the best match.

options.A: Grana are stacks of thylakoid membranes inside chloroplasts and need an electron microscope to resolve, you only see the whole chloroplast with light.
options.B: Lysosomes are too small and pale to be clearly seen at x400 with a simple light microscope, especially in plant cells.
options.C: Nucleoli are large, dense and stain strongly, so they show up clearly as dark spots inside the nucleus at x400.
options.D: Ribosomes are about 20 nm across, far below the 200 nm resolution limit of light, so they are invisible without an electron microscope.
